mastery_goal.title: Scientific Evidence and Relationships
mastery_goal.description: Use observations, evidence, testability, and models/relationships to build and evaluate physics explanations.

i_cans.exact_text: I can distinguish an observation from an inference.

families.label: Family A
families.name: Observation vs. Inference Classification
families.family_purpose: Separate what was directly observed from what was concluded.
families.exact_text: I can distinguish an observation from an inference.
families.student_action: Classify paired statements and justify the distinction.
families.evidence_job: Distinguish direct sensory/measurement evidence from interpretation.
forbidden_variations: change only names/nouns while preserving the same finished prompt
families.fresh_instance_rule: Preserve the evidence job and invariants; vary only declared axes. A fresh instance must not be a noun-only or number-only clone when conceptual reasoning is the evidence target.

exemplar.prompt: A student watches a cart roll across the floor. The student writes: “The cart traveled 2.4 m in 3.0 s” and “The wheels must have very little friction.” Classify each statement as an observation or an inference, and explain why.
exemplar.student_html:
A student watches a cart roll across the floor. The student writes:

  1. “The cart traveled 2.4 m in 3.0 s.”
  2. “The wheels must have very little friction.”

Classify each statement as an observation or an inference, and explain why.
exemplar.solution: The first statement reports measured quantities. The second proposes an explanation that was not directly observed.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Full credit requires both classifications and a distinction based on direct evidence versus interpretation.

families.label: Family B
families.name: Write One of Each
families.family_purpose: Produce an observation and an inference from the same evidence.
families.exact_text: I can distinguish an observation from an inference.
families.student_action: Read a small data record, then write one observation and one inference.
families.evidence_job: Show that the student can generate, not merely recognize, both categories.
invariants: data must support a clear direct statement and a plausible inference
variation_axes: ask for multiple observations before an inference
forbidden_variations: change only names/nouns while preserving the same finished prompt
families.fresh_instance_rule: Preserve the evidence job and invariants; vary only declared axes. A fresh instance must not be a noun-only or number-only clone when conceptual reasoning is the evidence target.

exemplar.prompt: A spring scale reading stays at 8 N for three trials. Write one observation supported directly by the record and one inference someone might reasonably make from it.
exemplar.student_html:
A spring scale gives the following readings:

TrialReading
18 N
28 N
38 N

Write one observation supported directly by the record and one inference someone might reasonably make from it.
exemplar.answer: Observation example: all three readings were 8 N. Inference example: the force was steady during the trials.
exemplar.solution: The observation repeats what the record directly shows; the inference interprets the pattern.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Observation must be directly supported; inference must go beyond the raw record without contradicting it.

families.label: Family C
families.name: Inference Disguised as Observation
families.family_purpose: Diagnose the common error of labeling an explanation as an observation.
families.exact_text: I can distinguish an observation from an inference.
families.student_action: Critique a student statement and rewrite it as a genuine observation.
families.evidence_job: Recognize when a statement smuggles interpretation into claimed observation.
invariants: the original statement must contain both observable evidence and an inferred cause
variation_axes: change the phenomenon and causal explanation
forbidden_variations: change only names/nouns while preserving the same finished prompt
families.fresh_instance_rule: Preserve the evidence job and invariants; vary only declared axes. A fresh instance must not be a noun-only or number-only clone when conceptual reasoning is the evidence target.

exemplar.prompt: A student says, “I observed that the block slowed down because friction was acting.” What part of that sentence is inference rather than observation? Rewrite the statement as an observation only.
exemplar.student_html:
A student says:

“I observed that the block slowed down because friction was acting.”

What part is an inference rather than an observation? Rewrite the statement as an observation only.
exemplar.answer: “because friction was acting” is the inference. A clean observation could be “The block’s speed decreased as it moved.”
exemplar.solution: Slowing can be observed/measured; the cause is an interpretation unless independently measured.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Identify the causal phrase as inference and provide a rewrite containing only observable/measurable information.

i_cans.exact_text: I can distinguish a hypothesis, scientific law, and scientific theory by what each does in science.

families.label: Family A
families.name: Scientific Explanation Roles
families.family_purpose: Distinguish hypothesis, law, and theory by function.
families.exact_text: I can distinguish a hypothesis, scientific law, and scientific theory by what each does in science.
families.student_action: Match descriptions to hypothesis, law, or theory.
families.evidence_job: Identify what each type of scientific statement does.
forbidden_variations: change only names/nouns while preserving the same finished prompt
families.fresh_instance_rule: Preserve the evidence job and invariants; vary only declared axes. A fresh instance must not be a noun-only or number-only clone when conceptual reasoning is the evidence target.

exemplar.prompt: Which term best fits each description: a testable proposed explanation; a concise statement of a repeated pattern in nature; a broad explanation supported by extensive evidence?
exemplar.student_html:
Match each description to hypothesis, scientific law, or scientific theory.

  1. A testable proposed explanation
  2. A concise statement of a repeated pattern in nature
  3. A broad explanation supported by extensive evidence
exemplar.solution: The three terms differ by role, not by a simple “guess-to-law” ladder.

families.label: Family B
families.name: Classify Statements by Role
families.family_purpose: Apply the terms to realistic scientific statements.
families.exact_text: I can distinguish a hypothesis, scientific law, and scientific theory by what each does in science.
families.evidence_job: Recognize the role a scientific statement is playing, not just recite definitions.
invariants: each example must clearly foreground the relevant role
variation_axes: swap in other testable proposals/patterns/explanatory frameworks
forbidden_variations: change only names/nouns while preserving the same finished prompt
families.fresh_instance_rule: Preserve the evidence job and invariants; vary only declared axes. A fresh instance must not be a noun-only or number-only clone when conceptual reasoning is the evidence target.

exemplar.prompt: Classify each as hypothesis, law, or theory: (1) “If surface roughness increases, a sliding block will slow more quickly.” (2) “For a given interaction, a measured pattern is summarized in a compact relationship.” (3) “A broad evidence-based model explains many related observations.”
exemplar.student_html:
Classify each statement as a hypothesis, scientific law, or scientific theory:

  1. “If surface roughness increases, a sliding block will slow more quickly.”
  2. “A repeated measured pattern is summarized in a compact relationship.”
  3. “A broad evidence-based model explains many related observations.”
exemplar.solution: The first is a testable proposal, the second summarizes a regularity, and the third explains a broad body of evidence.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Correctly classify each and justify at least one classification by function.

families.label: Family C
families.name: Theory Does Not Become Law
families.family_purpose: Target the misconception that theories “graduate” into laws.
families.exact_text: I can distinguish a hypothesis, scientific law, and scientific theory by what each does in science.
families.student_action: Evaluate a claim and correct it.
families.evidence_job: Explain why law and theory have different scientific jobs.
invariants: retain the misconception about hierarchy between law and theory
variation_axes: compare “law is more certain than theory”
forbidden_variations: change only names/nouns while preserving the same finished prompt
families.fresh_instance_rule: Preserve the evidence job and invariants; vary only declared axes. A fresh instance must not be a noun-only or number-only clone when conceptual reasoning is the evidence target.

exemplar.prompt: A classmate says, “A theory becomes a law once enough evidence proves it.” Explain what is wrong with this statement and describe the different jobs of laws and theories.
exemplar.student_html:
A classmate says:

“A theory becomes a law once enough evidence proves it.”

Explain what is wrong with this statement and describe the different jobs of laws and theories.
exemplar.answer: Laws summarize patterns/relationships; theories explain broad sets of observations. A theory does not become a law by accumulating evidence.
exemplar.solution: They are different kinds of scientific knowledge, not rungs on one ladder.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Must reject the graduation idea and correctly distinguish the roles.

i_cans.exact_text: I can decide whether a claim is testable and use evidence to judge whether the claim is supported.

families.label: Family A
families.name: Testable Claim + Evidence
families.family_purpose: Judge whether evidence supports a testable claim.
families.exact_text: I can decide whether a claim is testable and use evidence to judge whether the claim is supported.
families.student_action: Identify what is testable and compare evidence to the prediction.
families.evidence_job: Use a defined observation to evaluate a claim.
invariants: evidence directly bears on the claim
variation_axes: include evidence that contradicts or is mixed
forbidden_variations: change only names/nouns while preserving the same finished prompt
families.fresh_instance_rule: Preserve the evidence job and invariants; vary only declared axes. A fresh instance must not be a noun-only or number-only clone when conceptual reasoning is the evidence target.

exemplar.prompt: Claim: “Increasing the pull on the same cart makes its motion change more during the same time interval.” Three trials use pulls of 2 N, 4 N, and 6 N, and the measured speed changes are 0.4, 0.8, and 1.2 m/s. Is the claim testable, and does this evidence support it?
exemplar.student_html:
Claim: Increasing the pull on the same cart makes its motion change more during the same time interval.

PullChange in speed
2 N0.4 m/s
4 N0.8 m/s
6 N1.2 m/s

Is the claim testable? Does this evidence support it? Explain.
exemplar.answer: Yes; it predicts a measurable relationship, and the data support the claim because larger pulls are paired with larger changes in speed.
exemplar.solution: A testable claim must connect to an observable measurement; the trend is consistent with the claim.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: State testability, verdict, and cite the relevant trend.

families.label: Family B
families.name: Design a Test
families.family_purpose: Turn a claim into a measurable test.
families.exact_text: I can decide whether a claim is testable and use evidence to judge whether the claim is supported.
families.student_action: Specify what to change, what to measure, and what result would matter.
families.evidence_job: Identify a measurement that could confirm or challenge the claim.
invariants: claim must be testable with accessible observations
variation_axes: vary whether student chooses measurement or comparison
forbidden_variations: change only names/nouns while preserving the same finished prompt
families.fresh_instance_rule: Preserve the evidence job and invariants; vary only declared axes. A fresh instance must not be a noun-only or number-only clone when conceptual reasoning is the evidence target.

exemplar.prompt: Claim: “A heavier book has more inertia than a lighter book.” Describe a simple test that would collect evidence relevant to the claim. State what you would compare or measure.
exemplar.student_html:
Claim: “A heavier book has more inertia than a lighter book.”

Describe a simple test that would collect evidence relevant to the claim. State what you would compare or measure. You do not need to carry out the test.
exemplar.answer: Example: apply comparable pushes to books of different mass and compare how difficult it is to change their motion, while keeping the interaction as consistent as possible.
exemplar.solution: A useful test links the claim to observable evidence and identifies a comparison.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Plan must identify a measurable/observable comparison relevant to inertia and avoid circular reasoning.

families.label: Family C
families.name: Evidence That Does Not Test the Claim
families.exact_text: I can decide whether a claim is testable and use evidence to judge whether the claim is supported.
families.student_action: Evaluate two evidence sets and explain which actually tests the claim.
families.evidence_job: Distinguish evidence that bears on the claim from evidence that merely sounds scientific.
invariants: one evidence set must directly test the claim and one must not
variation_axes: ask what additional evidence is needed
forbidden_variations: change only names/nouns while preserving the same finished prompt
families.fresh_instance_rule: Preserve the evidence job and invariants; vary only declared axes. A fresh instance must not be a noun-only or number-only clone when conceptual reasoning is the evidence target.

exemplar.prompt: Claim: “The support force on a resting book points upward.” Student A measures the book’s mass. Student B uses a force sensor between the book and table to determine the direction of the contact force. Whose evidence is more directly relevant to the claim, and why?
exemplar.student_html:
Claim: “The support force on a resting book points upward.”

  • Student A measures the book’s mass.
  • Student B uses a force sensor/contact setup to determine the direction of the table’s force on the book.

Whose evidence is more directly relevant to the claim, and why?
exemplar.answer: Student B, because the evidence addresses the direction of the contact/support force itself.
exemplar.solution: Mass alone does not establish the direction of the support force.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Choose B and explain relevance to the actual claim.

i_cans.exact_text: I can explain what a formula or model says about the relationship between physical quantities.

families.label: Family A
families.name: Read a Relationship
families.exact_text: I can explain what a formula or model says about the relationship between physical quantities.
families.student_action: Translate a simple net-force relationship into words.
families.evidence_job: Explain what a relationship says about physical quantities without merely calculating.
invariants: student must interpret the relationship physically
variation_axes: change force values only as support, not the core task
ask effect of increasing one term
forbidden_variations: change only names/nouns while preserving the same finished prompt
families.fresh_instance_rule: Preserve the evidence job and invariants; vary only declared axes. A fresh instance must not be a noun-only or number-only clone when conceptual reasoning is the evidence target.

exemplar.prompt: For horizontal forces in opposite directions, a model is F_net = F_right − F_left. What does this relationship say about how the two forces determine the net force?
exemplar.student_html:
For horizontal forces in opposite directions, consider the model:

\(F_{net}=F_{right}-F_{left}\)

Explain in words what this relationship says about how the two forces determine the net force.
exemplar.answer: The net horizontal force depends on the difference between the opposing forces; equal forces give zero net force, and the larger side sets the net direction.
exemplar.solution: Interpret subtraction as opposition, not as a plug-in instruction only.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Explain both difference and the physical meaning of equality/larger side.

families.label: Family B
families.name: Predict a Change from the Model
families.family_purpose: Use a relationship to make a qualitative prediction.
families.exact_text: I can explain what a formula or model says about the relationship between physical quantities.
families.student_action: Predict the effect of changing one force while another stays fixed.
families.evidence_job: Reason about how changing one quantity changes the represented result.
invariants: one term changes while the other is controlled
forbidden_variations: change only names/nouns while preserving the same finished prompt
families.fresh_instance_rule: Preserve the evidence job and invariants; vary only declared axes. A fresh instance must not be a noun-only or number-only clone when conceptual reasoning is the evidence target.

exemplar.prompt: A cart has opposing horizontal forces. F_left stays 5 N while F_right increases from 5 N to 9 N. Without treating the formula as a plug-in exercise, describe how the net force changes and what feature of the relationship tells you that.
exemplar.student_html:
A cart has opposing horizontal forces described by \(F_{net}=F_{right}-F_{left}\).

\(F_{left}\) stays at 5 N while \(F_{right}\) increases from 5 N to 9 N.

Describe how the net force changes and what feature of the relationship tells you that.
exemplar.answer: It changes from zero to 4 N right because increasing the rightward term makes the difference positive/rightward.
exemplar.solution: The change follows from the difference between opposing contributions.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Correct qualitative/quantitative change plus explanation tied to the relationship.

families.label: Family C
families.name: Formula as Thinking Tool
families.exact_text: I can explain what a formula or model says about the relationship between physical quantities.
families.student_action: Critique a student who says a formula has no meaning until numbers are inserted.
families.evidence_job: Explain what information a formula communicates beyond an answer.
invariants: response must interpret structure without requiring calculation
variation_axes: ask for prediction or limiting case
forbidden_variations: change only names/nouns while preserving the same finished prompt
families.fresh_instance_rule: Preserve the evidence job and invariants; vary only declared axes. A fresh instance must not be a noun-only or number-only clone when conceptual reasoning is the evidence target.

exemplar.prompt: A student says, “The equation F_net = F_right − F_left tells me nothing until I have numbers to plug in.” Explain two things the equation already tells you before any numbers are used.
exemplar.student_html:
A student says:

“The equation \(F_{net}=F_{right}-F_{left}\) tells me nothing until I have numbers to plug in.”

Explain two things the relationship already tells you before any numbers are used.
exemplar.answer: Examples: the forces oppose each other; the net depends on their difference; equal opposing forces give zero net force; the larger force determines the net direction.
exemplar.solution: The symbolic model encodes structure and physical relationships before numerical substitution.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Give two correct physical interpretations of the relationship.
